title: MC0-09037
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Haiti, is appealing the negative decision rendered in his claim by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on XXXX XXXX, 2020.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Haiti, is appealing the negative decision rendered in his claim by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on XXXX XXXX, 2020.

The determinative issue for the RPD was credibility. The RPD found that the Appellant was not credible in his allegations that he was targeted and threatened by gang members in XXXX 2017 after failing to provide a payment out of a group savings plan with other merchants; that his home and car were shot at and his home ransacked in XXXX 2017; that he made complaints to authorities regarding these events; and that his wife was threatened by the gang in XXXX2017 and XXXX2018.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its negative credibility findings that resulted from a microscopic analysis. The Appellant also argues that there was a violation of the fundamental principles of justice, as the RPD demonstrated bias and entered into evidence an exhibit that the Appellant did not wish to produce. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in failing to conduct an analysis under s97, state protection or internal flight alternative.

I find that the RPD erred in its negative credibility findings. I do not find that there was evidence of bias on the part of the RPD and noted that the Appellant did not provide any indication during the RPD hearing that he did not wish to enter the particular exhibit into evidence. I therefore do not find that there was a violation of procedural fairness. As the RPD erred in its credibility findings, I find that it also erred in not conducting an analysis under s97, state protection or internal flight alternative (IFA).

I find that the Appellant has produced credible evidence that, on the balance of probabilities, he faces a risk to life that is personal and one that is not generally faced by others in Haiti in accordance with section 97(1)(b) of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA); that he has rebutted the presumption of adequate state protection in Haiti; and that there is no viable internal flight alternative for the Appellant in Haiti.
The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a "person in need of protection" in accordance with section 97(1)(b) of IRPA.
No new evidence has been provided to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) and there has been no request for an oral hearing.

When reviewing the RPD decision, I independently assessed the evidence, including listening to the audio recording of the RPD hearing of February 11, 2020, and reviewing the transcript, to determine whether or not the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, of fact, or of mixed law and fact. ANALYSIS Nexus to the Convention

As the allegations of the Appellant do not give rise to Convention grounds, I shall examine the allegations in light of s 97 of IRPA. Credibility Threats of XXXX XXXX, 2017: Contradiction between Appellant's testimony and the complaint

The RPD found that the Appellant's credibility was undermined by the difference between the date on which he alleged that he had prepared a complaint with his lawyer regarding the threats received by a gang leader on XXXX XXXX, 2017, which he testified had been the same day, and the information in the complaint filed with authorities1, which indicated that the complaint had been prepared on XXXX XXXX, 2017. Although the complaint was dated and signed on XXXX XXXX, 2017 regarding the XXXX XXXX, 2017 incident, the Appellant had testified that he had been out of the country on that date, as was indicated in his passport, and said that maybe the date had been an administrative error, or that maybe it represented the date it had been delivered to the magistrate. The RPD was not satisfied by the explanation of the Appellant, as the document appeared to have been signed by the Appellant and his lawyer on the date of XXXX XXXX, 2017, but notations in the margin indicated that it was received on that date and a stamp on the document also bears that date. The RPD therefore found that the credibility of the Appellant was undermined regarding the alleged XXXX XXXX, 2017 incident and awarded no weight to the document.
The Appellant submits that this is a contradiction that he cannot explain, but argues that the RPD erred in not giving him the opportunity to provide an explanation during the hearing.

I find that the RPD did not err in failing to give the Appellant the opportunity to explain during the hearing, because it did do so, clearly asking the Appellant why the document indicated the date of XXXX XXXXwhen the Appellant had testified that the complaint had been signed on the XXXX, and the Appellant answered that maybe it was a mistake of the magistrate or an administrative error, because he had been in the U.S on that date2. However, I find that the RPD did err in giving the document no weight and in finding that the Appellant's credibility was undermined by this contradiction.

The document in question, a complaint prepared by the Appellant's lawyer and then registered with a magistrate, is extremely detailed and provides information that is corroborated by both testimony and the Basis of Claim Form (BOC). It includes identifying information about the Appellant, his lawyer, the prosecutor's office that received the complaint, the circumstances that led to the threats of the Appellant by the gang leader, a quotation in Creole (for which translation was provided) of the threat by the gang leader to the Appellant, as well as a reference to the specific legislative provisions that are applicable regarding the threats.

I consider that this one element of the date of the document, which differs by a matter of days from that testified to by the Appellant-who immediately said that he could not have signed on that date of XXXX XXXXbecause he was out of the country, as corroborated by his passport-and who did not try to embellish or invent an answer but spontaneously provided testimony, should not outweigh the detailed information provided in the document or in the BOC narrative or testimony. I find that the document merits weight in establishing the Appellant's allegations, and the unexplained discrepancy of the date should not undermine his credibility. Incident of XXXX XXXX, 2017

The RPD found that documents D-5 and D-6, which were complaints regarding the alleged incident of XXXX XXXX, 2017, merited no weight, and that the Appellant had not established that this incident had a link with the alleged threats against him by the gang leader, for the reasons as set out below.

The Appellant argues that the RPD undertook a microscopic examination of the differences between the documents and the information in the BOC and testimony in reaching a negative credibility finding, and used circular reasoning to reject the allegations because it had rejected the documents; therefore the RPD erred.

I find that the RPD erred in awarding no weight to the documents and in reaching a negative credibility finding concerning the link of this event to the threats against the Appellant by the gang leader, for the reasons as set out below. Incident of XXXX XXXX, 2017: Terminology used in BOC different from that used in testimony

The RPD found that the credibility of the Appellant was mitigated by what it saw as different terminology used to describe the same incident in the BOC versus that which was used during the Appellant's testimony. The RPD considered that the use of the word "fouiller" to describe the actions of the gang members in the Appellant's house on XXXX XXXX, 2017 when describing the incident in his BOC, was different from the word "saccager" used during his testimony to describe the actions by the gang members in his house. The RPD asked the Appellant why he had only alleged in his BOC that his house had been searched by the bandits, without mentioning specifically that anything had been destroyed, but that during his testimony he had said that the bandits had destroyed some of the items in his house. The Appellant replied that the word he used in his BOC, "fouiller" meant the same thing as "saccager" and implied that the bandits had caused damage inside the house. The RPD found that this explanation was not satisfactory and concluded that the Appellant's credibility was undermined as a result.

The Appellant argues that when evaluating the credibility of a claimant, different factors that can affect testimony should be taken into consideration and the RPD erred in failing to do so. The Appellant submits that cultural differences, differences in language expressions, use of synonyms, the fact that an interpreter from Creole to French was used both at the hearing and in writing the BOC narrative, should all be taken into consideration in this situation, as well as the dictionary definitions of the words in question, when assessing the credibility of the Appellant for the apparent differences in the words used. The Appellant submits that the dictionary definitions of the words "saccager" and "fouiller" are not contradictory because "fouiller" means to search while creating disorder and not caring if damage is caused, while "saccager" means to destroy.

I find that the RPD erred in considering that the use of different words by the Appellant to describe the XXXX XXXX, 2017 incident undermined his credibility, as I find that the words themselves are very similar. If one word means to be indifferent if damage is caused while searching through the home, while the other means that damage was caused in a more intentional way, I find that those meanings are sufficiently close as not to be considered a contradiction. When I additionally consider that the Appellant was assisted by a Creole-French interpreter at the hearing and in his BOC, such that the words used are being translated from one language to another and the Appellant's use of words must be considered in that context, I agree with the submissions of the Appellant in this regard. During the hearing, the RPD asked the Appellant to explain why in the BOC it said that the bandits had "fouillé" his house but during his testimony, he had said that they had damaged items in the house, and he replied that it was the same thing, as he was referring to the bandits searching through his home, taking what they wanted and causing damage3. I consider the words to be synonymous and find that the RPD erred in considering that these were of such a difference as to be contradictory and undermine the Appellant's credibility. I find that the Appellant's credibility regarding the allegations of XXXX XXXX, 2017 is not undermined as a result. Incident of XXXX XXXX, 2017: Contradictions regarding what Appellant could see

The RPD found that the credibility of the Appellant was undermined by the differences in his testimony regarding his observations of the agents of harm on XXXX XXXX, 2017. The RPD considered that the Appellant had indicated originally that he had seen people, but did not recognize them, but later in his testimony had said that there was no electricity and that nothing could be seen. The RPD found that because the Appellant had not provided a reasonable explanation for this contradiction, he did not establish on the balance of probabilities that the break-in to his house on XXXX XXXX, 2017 had been orchestrated by the particular alleged gang leader.

The Appellant argues that the fact that there was no electricity meant that he could not clearly see people in the house, but there would still have been some natural illumination from the stars and moon, such that he was able to see something. The Appellant submits that he therefore did not contradict himself. Furthermore, the Appellant submits that even though he could not clearly see the individuals in his house, it was established that on the balance of probabilities, it was an action orchestrated by the gang leader, as he had no problems prior to the threats by the gang leader to extort a portion of the balance owing from his group savings with the other merchants, and the gang leader had specifically made reference to the upcoming payment that the Appellant was expecting, following which his house was broken into the night he received the payment.

In his BOC, the Appellant indicated that during the incident, he had left from the back of his house and hidden behind a bush in his neighbour's yard, during which time he saw men that he did not know inside his house4. During his testimony, the RPD confronted the Appellant with the fact that earlier in his testimony, he had said that he hadn't seen the men prior to making a complaint against them and identifying the gang leader in his complaint. The Appellant replied that it was impossible to identify the men in his house because it was late at night and in Haiti at that time there was a power outage5. I do not find that there is any contradiction, and I find that the RPD erred in considering that this impugned his credibility, because whether or not the Appellant saw the men who broke into his house a little bit or not at all, either way he did not recognize them, and his reason for accusing the gang leader was not based on his visual observation during the incident but on the fact that unknown people had broken into his home and threatened him, after firing gunshots. In the Appellant's BOC, he had written that one of the bandits had addressed him by his first name and said that he could hide, but that they would find him6. It was the Appellant's belief that it was the gang leader for the reasons already explained. I find that the Appellant has met his standard of proof of the balance of probabilities, with respect to the identity of the individuals who broke into his house, shot outside his house and threatened him on XXXX XXXX, 2017, based on the previous threats by the gang leader and the fact that the break-in occurred when he was expected to receive his money. I consider that, given the credible evidence provided by the Appellant, it is more probable than not that the individuals who broke into his house were there in connection with the gang leader's threats, and I therefore find that the RPD erred in finding that the break-in had not been orchestrated by the gang leader. Incident of XXXX XXXX, 2017: Omissions in exhibits regarding theft of money or damage inside house

The RPD found that the Appellant's credibility was undermined by the omission from his complaint following the alleged XXXX XXXX, 2017 incident of the theft of money from his home or the destruction of items inside his house7. When the RPD confronted the Appellant about this omission, he replied during the hearing that the magistrate had not noted all the information and that it was possible that he had omitted that, explaining that to him it was logical that the bandits would have been looking for money if they were breaking into his house. The RPD found that this explanation was unsatisfactory and that, as the stolen money was at the heart of his allegations, its omission from the complaint with the justice of the peace8 and from the extract of the minutes of the clerk9 undermines his credibility.

The Appellant argues that even if the complaints do not specifically mention that the money was stolen, they do indicate that the bandits had entered the house to take money, "emporter l'argent", and that there is no difference between saying that they had entered the house to take money or that they had stolen money. Furthermore, the Appellant submits that the allegation of the money having been stolen during the break-in is indicated in the BOC narrative. The Appellant therefore argues that the RPD erred in reaching a negative credibility finding in this regard.

I find that the RPD erred in making a negative credibility finding due to the apparent omission from the documents, as I do not find that there was an omission in those documents. Exhibit D-5, which is a complaint that was prepared by the Appellant's lawyer in Haiti and addressed to a justice of the peace in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, indicates that the bandits on the night of XXXX XXXX, 2017, entered the Appellant's house to assassinate him and steal money, as they expected that he had XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in Haitian currency at the house10. Exhibit D-6, which is an extract of the minutes of the clerk of the justice of the peace of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, contains the same information11. During the hearing, the RPD had confronted the Appellant and asked why the complaint does not really mention that the bandits had taken money, it just says that they were looking for money, and the Appellant replied that it could have happened that they had forgotten to put in everything that he had said, but that the bandits were coming to his house for a reason, it was logical that they wanted to take something12. In his BOC, it is indicated that the next morning, he realized that they had stolen money13. I consider that the information in the exhibits indicates the intention of the bandits to steal money, which combined with the testimony of the Appellant and the information in the BOC, is consistent and corroborates the allegations of the Appellant regarding the incident of XXXX XXXX, 2017, such that the allegations have been established on the balance of probabilities. Incident of XXXX XXXX, 2017: Omission regarding damage to car

The RPD found that the Appellant's credibility was adversely affected by the omission in his BOC of the allegation in the complaints14 that his car had sustained damage from bullets during the XXXX XXXX, 2017 incident. During the hearing, the RPD asked the Appellant about this and he replied that it was his car that was damaged and that he could not explain why he had left this out of his BOC. Also, the RPD found that the Appellant's credibility was lessened by the omission of this during his testimony, as when he was asked if anything besides the ransacking of his house had happened during this event, he answered no.

The Appellant argues that even if the BOC did not mention that his car had been hit by bullets, he had written in the BOC that he had heard gunshots, such that the fact that the car was damaged by the gunshots was a mere detail, the omission of which should not impugn his credibility.

In the Appellant's BOC, he wrote that on XXXX XXXX, 2017, after knocks at his door late at night, to which he did not answer, he heard gunshots15. In Exhibit D-6, the extract of the minutes of the clerk for the justice of the peace of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, it is indicated that a justice of the peace went to the home of the Appellant on XXXX XXXX, 2017 to observe and document the damage that had been sustained after the event of XXXX XXXX, 2017. Aside from noting bullet holes in the front door and wall of the house, the justice of the peace also noted that a white car, which was identified by its licence plate, manufacturer and model, had bullet holes in the front and rear windows, as well as five cartridges from bullets in the alley near the house16. During the hearing, the RPD asked the Appellant who owned the car that was mentioned in this report and the Appellant replied that he did, that he used it to drive his wife and children. When he was asked why he had not mentioned in his BOC that the car had been shot at, he answered that it was in the complaint17. I find that the RPD erred in impugning his credibility due to the omission from his BOC and testimony of this information, because I consider that the allegation that the Appellant's car, which was parked near his house, would have been damaged by bullets is consistent with his allegations in his BOC and testimony that he had heard gunshots outside his house that night. Also, the information was documented in the report of the justice of the peace in a detailed fashion, while also corroborating the other allegations of that night. Complaints by Appellant's wife

The RPD found that the Appellant's credibility was undermined by the omission in one document of information that appeared in another document, regarding complaints that the Appellant's wife had made following threats by the gang leader to her, after the Appellant had left Haiti. In one document dated XXXX XXXX, 2018, prepared by the Appellant's lawyer in Haiti and addressed to a justice of the peace, there is a complaint that on XXXX XXXX, 2018, the gang leader threatened his wife at the store and asked for the Appellant18. In another document dated XXXX XXXX, 2018, prepared by the Appellant's lawyer in Haiti and addressed to the prosecutor's office, there is the same information as in the previous complaint with the additional mention that the Appellant's wife had given the bandits money so that they would leave19. The RPD considered that the omission of this information from one of the complaints, combined with the address on the complaints as being the Appellant's original address in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, even though he had testified that she had been in hiding in XXXX at that time, undermined the credibility of the Appellant and the probative value of the two complaints. The RPD therefore found that the Appellant had not established on the balance of probabilities that his wife had been threatened by the gang leader.

The Appellant argues that the second document with the additional information was not intended to have been put into evidence and that the RPD put too much emphasis on a small detail that was in a document from a country that is known not to have rigorous judicial writings, according to the objective documentary evidence.

I find that the RPD erred in reaching a negative credibility finding regarding the allegation of threats against the Appellant's wife based on the address of the documents and the addition of one element in one of the reports. I consider that the testimony of the Appellant, his BOC and the forms he filled out all indicate that his wife was hiding with the children in another location, that they owned the house in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXbut that they no longer occupy it, and I find that this outweighs the fact that her address in the complaints was indicated as being the official family residence in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Furthermore, I consider the addition of the allegation that the Appellant's wife had provided money to the gang leader so that they would leave the store as being peripheral and its omission from one document not a credibility concern. I find that these documents have weight for the allegation that the Appellant's wife was threatened and that the gang leader was still looking for the Appellant after he had left Haiti. Evidence in Exhibits not discussed in RPD decision

The RPD decision did not discuss the detailed information contained in Exhibits D-5, D-6 and D-7, except to point out the omissions that they either contained or that they represented in the Appellant's testimony. However, I find that after reviewing them carefully, they merit high weight in establishing the allegations of the Appellant, as they contain many specific, identifying details about the Appellant, the lawyers who prepared the complaints, the observations of the Appellant, his wife, and a justice of the peace regarding the various incidents, including contact information and relevant legislative provisions of the various offences. Exhibit D-11 is a letter from the Appellant's lawyer in Haiti that indicates that his file is still open, but that as of February 2020, no follow-up has been made by the judicial authorities. Conclusion on Credibility

I find that the Appellant is credible and has established, on the balance of probabilities, that he was targeted by gang members after failing to provide a payment out of a group savings plan with other merchants, which the gang leader had threatened him to provide on XXXX XXXX, 2017; that he made a complaint to authorities regarding this threat; that on XXXX XXXX, 2017, after receiving the payment in question, gunshots were fired at his home and at his car, his home was broken into and ransacked, and money was stolen by unidentified individuals that he has established on the balance of probabilities were connected to the gang leader who had threatened him; that he made another complaint to authorities regarding this incident; that subsequently he went into hiding; that in XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, his wife was threatened by the same gang leader at the store who said that he would find the Appellant; that after the Appellant left Haiti, his wife was again threatened by the gang leader in XXXX 2018; that as of XXXX 2020, the lawyer of the Appellant in Haiti indicated that the file is still open but that no further legal action has been taken regarding his complaints.

Based on the credible evidence provided by the Appellant regarding the existence of the agents of harm, the fact that they have targeted him and threatened his wife recently, and the objective documentary evidence that indicates that gang members take vengeance for reporting them to police and that they commonly target family members of those who have wronged them,20 I therefore find that the Appellant faces, on the balance of probabilities, a risk to his life that is personal and one that is not generally faced by others, as he has been particularly targeted by gang members who have tried to take vengeance against him because he had refused to provide them with payment and had contacted the authorities through his lawyer to report that he had been threatened by a gang leader, then had his home shot at and ransacked, money stolen, received further threats and did further reporting to authorities, and recent threats were made to his wife. The fact that gunshots were fired at his home and his car, followed by repeated threats directed at him personally and his repeatedly reporting the agent of harm to the authorities indicates the serious and dangerous nature of the threats and their repeated and personal targeting of the Appellant, such that I find this is a risk that is not generally faced by others in Haiti.

The objective documentary evidence shows that acts of revenge may be committed by gangs for collaborating with police, with one source reporting that those who report criminals to the police are "particularly targeted".21 While one assistant professor indicates that the severity and likelihood of an act of revenge reduce over time, in relation to the distance from and power of a particular gang,22 I find that the standard of proof for a risk to the Appellant's life is met, on a balance of probabilities, based on the number of incidents in which he and his wife were threatened, the seriousness of the act of the agents of harm having shot multiple times at the Appellant's house and car, and the fact that the incidents had taken place repeatedly over the years.

I find that the Appellant has established, on the balance of probabilities, that he faces a risk to life that is personal, and one that is not generally faced by others, if he were to return to Haiti, in accordance with s 97(1) of IRPA. State Protection

The Appellant has provided credible evidence that he sought the help of authorities after he was threatened by a gang leader, then again when his house was shot at, then again by his wife after she was threatened, but that he continues to be targeted and that no action has been taken by police.

According to the national documentary evidence, there is a lack of state protection in Haiti. Specifically, country conditions indicate that the Haitian police force does not have enough personnel or resources to meet the requirements of the population.23 Police are described as being incapable of defending the population against organized or informal crime.24 Furthermore, abuses by police tend to go unpunished.25 In addition, the justice system has been described as ineffective and corrupt, and country conditions indicate that high-ranking security officials have links to organized crime.26

After assessing the personal and objective documentary evidence of the Appellant, I find that he has rebutted the presumption of adequate state protection with clear and convincing evidence, that if he were to seek state protection, the authorities of Haiti would be unwilling or unable to provide it. IFA

The Appellant provided credible evidence that the agents of harm had threatened him and shot at his home, then continued to threaten his wife after he left Haiti, over several years. Specifically, he testified that his wife and children have been forced to live in hiding and that it is only because they are in hiding that the agent of harm has not found them27; the Appellant also testified that Haiti is a small and impoverished country, such that for a small amount of money the gang leader could easily obtain information about his whereabouts, in exchange for payment, if he were to try to relocate28; He estimated that if he were to try to relocate to Cap Haitien for example, the agent of harm would likely be able to find him within a matter of weeks, such that there is nowhere in Haiti that he could safely relocate29; the Appellant testified that the agent of harm has connections in various towns in Haiti, that he does not work alone30. I find that, on the balance of probabilities, given the credible testimony by the Appellant regarding the ability and interest of the agents of harm to track him down in Haiti, specifically the repeated threats over the years to the Appellant's wife and the gang leader's connections; combined with the lack of adequate state protection in Haiti for the Appellant; that the agents of harm would have the means and motivation to find the Appellant throughout Haiti and that, as a result, there is nowhere in Haiti that would be safe for him to relocate.
I find that the Appellant has established that on the balance of probabilities, he faces a risk to life that is personal and one that is not generally faced by others, should he return to Haiti.

The appeal is allowed. The RPD decision is set aside. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a "person in need of protection" in accordance with s 97 (1)(b) of IRPA.
